utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Well, I noted that down when their patrols passed by and when they had their drills and I met them, I met some -- about 30 of them, and they were all people, Muslims, from Donja Veceriska. I know them all and I saw the weapons they were carrying; and when they would go up to the frontline with the Serbs towards Visoko, Cekrcici, then one platoon would go up to that line, there were some ten members of it, 30 or 40 of them, and they were carrying rifles and full military gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you noted these 55 people carrying arms, was that before your injury or after your injury?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: It was after my injury, when I returned home. Before this injury, we were almost equal as to the number of weapons. They had six or seven rifles just as we did, up until the time that I was wounded; and later on, they had more weapons than we did. They were better armed than we were. I can say that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you make an inventory of the number of weapons that were in the possession of the Bosnian Croats in Donja Veceriska from December 1992 until April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You already asked that question, Mr. Harmon; at least it seems to me you have already answered it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some additional questions. I'd like to show you Defence Exhibit 537A, all right? If I could have the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Look at the clock. I have asked the registrar to see how much time there is. You know, there is still the cross-examination. The interpreters are prepared to stay a little bit longer, but I would like to be able to finish our work today so that we can begin the direct examination of the accused tomorrow. How much time is left for the Prosecution? Ten minutes maximum?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No more than fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. No more than fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will keep in mind the time frame, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to item number 4 on this particular document. First of all, Mr. Lovric, have you seen this document before coming into the courtroom to testify, and if so, when did you first see this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I was present when it was written because they are all my friends, the commander and the members.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at this particular meeting -- first of all, can you identify the extreme individuals on the Croat side? What does this document, item number 4, refer to, and who does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: The units of the reserve force of Donja Veceriska and the Muslim army should take over control considering the extreme individuals on both sides. As far as the Croats are concerned, from Donja Veceriska, I personally consider that there were no extremists there because they never performed any kind of extremist incident to the Muslims. However, the Muslims usually considered that a man was extremist, had extremist leanings, when the Muslims said that the time would come when they would sleep with the Croat women in the village, and if the Croat would say that that time would never come or that the time will never come for us to wear fezzes and say Lahko and Mehko, the type of Muslim talk, then they would consider that person to be an extremist, but I don't think those were extremists. Extremists are those who shot round the village and threw bombs, and this is something that the Muslims themselves did, and Fehret Haskic was foremost among these as an extremist of the ultra-extremist type. Ferid Kalca as well; he was a specialist in the making of explosives. He was able to make pistols and all sorts of weapons and to lay the explosives. This was an exceptionally dangerous trio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, on the evening of the 15th, you said that the civilian Croat population was ordered to evacuate the village, and indeed they did that. They went up to, I think, Gornja Veceriska, the Croatian part of the village, and that you personally left around 2.30 in the morning on the morning of the 16th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they were ordered to go to the upper part of the Croatian village and that part of them went to Gornja Veceriska straightaway, the civilians, and part of the civilians remained and then left when the fighting started. I myself did go around 2.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Lovric: Did any soldiers of the HVO, from outside the village of Donja Veceriska, come into the village of Donja Veceriska prior to your departure on the morning of the 16th at 2.30 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No, they did not come before, but when the fighting started in Donja Veceriska, they then came to help out some of the young men from Gornja Veceriska, from Mosunj, and some 15 young men from Nova Bila who belonged to the Tvrtko company, so that a sort of balance was struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see the people who were members of the HVO from outside your village come to your village?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No, because I had gone up to Gornja Veceriska, and I returned on the 18th at about noon, and there were no foreign soldiers when I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had there been?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had there been any soldiers from outside of Donja Veceriska who were members of the HVO in the days that you were outside of the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No, not on that particular night, but when the fighting started, then there were only the members from Donja Veceriska, and they took up the fighting, and then young men from Gornja Veceriska arrived and from Mosunj and Nova Bila, they arrived to help out. How many there were, rumour had it that there were about 15 Tvrtkovci, whereas I don't know how many from Donja Veceriska there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you see any of the HVO soldiers at all during the two days of fighting that took place at Donja Veceriska? I understand, Mr. Lovric, that you were at a different vantage point. You were up at Gornja Veceriska. But looking down, could you see any members of the HVO engaged in fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't see any individuals because Gornja Veceriska is about two kilometres away, two to two and a half kilometres from my vantage point, so it was impossible to make out and distinguish a man. You could only see houses, and they would look like small houses, very small dots, and you couldn't make out the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in Defence Exhibit 538 -- did you prepare this diagram yourself?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with the help of my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you prepare this particular diagram?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: The diagram. When I passed on the 18th of April, I marked in what had burnt down during the fighting because I kept records on my own, and I drew up this diagram about -- several months ago. I don't quite remember. Several months ago. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on this diagram, Mr. Lovric, I count approximately 42 Muslim homes that are burned or partially destroyed and I count 11 Croat houses that are burned or partially destroyed. Did you see any of those houses set afire?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I saw smoke during the combat operations in this part here (indicating), that's the street I live on, and you can see this from Upper Veceriska, Gornja Veceriska, and it's just as if it was on the palm of your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I take it you don't know the circumstances under which any of these houses were set afire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: These Muslim houses were burning in the combat operation zone, these here, whereas these other ones were in the background, these here (indicating), then two houses belonging to the Miskovic family. This is well in the rear, and this was intentionally set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I take it when you returned home on the afternoon or at noon on the 18th of April, the fighting had completely terminated in Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it further from your testimony that all but nine of the Muslim residents of Donja Veceriska had fled the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say "fled." They withdrew. They went with UNPROFOR, the army withdrew following them, and during those two days of fighting, the HVO soldiers came up to the Lovric houses, which means that this was still under the control of the -- that the Muslims had control, Besic and the Brdo area, and we thought it was strange --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Lovric, let me interrupt you for just a second. I don't mean to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Harmon. Then I want to ask Mr. Nobilo if he has any further questions to ask. So please ask your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I have to make a selection of which will be my last question -- if I could have, with the Court's indulgence, a few more questions, Mr. President, I would appreciate it. I will be finished within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. The interpreters are doing additional work this evening. We have to take into account what was decided this morning. Perhaps the Judges have some questions to ask. I hope that Mr. Nobilo will be brief in his redirect. You have one more question, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear that Dario Kordic was in your village on the night of the 15th of April, 1993, at the cafe that belonged to Mr. Drmic?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: He was not in Donja Veceriska at all on that day. Only during the war did Dario Kordic come to Donja Veceriska once. Perhaps half a year before the war broke out. I don't remember exactly when that was. But he was not there on that evening. That is a disinformation. It is a lie. I say that categorically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I think that's all. Mr. Nobilo, you can have redirect time now, but be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Turning to my colleagues. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Lovric, I understood you to be saying that some Croat houses at the back of the village were intentionally set afire.

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But that the Muslim houses were destroyed in the course of a conflict; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Fourteen Muslim houses were burnt down during the fighting in the combat operation zone, or 14 of them, whereas the Croatian houses -- you saw the map and you saw the positions of the Croatian houses -- they were well into the back of the territory under Muslim control and they were intentionally set fire to. My house was also looted. They took things away. I wanted to open a small shop, and I kept my goods there, and so along the road, I found many of the things from my shop there. A house can burn down but you cannot -- the screen of a television set cannot burn down. What do I want to say? What I want to say is that they thought they were stronger and that they would wipe us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I asked you a question. The point of the question was to clarify your answer. Do you confirm that your testimony is that the Croat houses were burnt down intentionally but that the Muslim houses were destroyed in the course of the conflict? Was that your testimony, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Croatian houses were intentionally burnt down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well now, were any Croatian houses destroyed in the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were any Muslim houses intentionally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of how the fighting developed, and whether some were intentionally destroyed or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I take your answer to be that some Muslim houses may or may not have been intentionally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I don't think any of these houses were intentionally destroyed because a house can be set fire to in the zone, the fighting zone; for example, the shed catches fire and then-- with a bullet or a bomb or anything of that kind and then the house catches fire as well. But our men were not able to reach those houses when they were on fire. They didn't reach the houses, which meant that they were set fire to during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is your testimony then that so far as you knew, no Muslim houses were intentionally set afire?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: During the combat operations, no, and after the fighting, some eight houses were set on fire. Somebody did that, some unknown perpetrator did this intentionally. I said that in the course of my testimony. In addition to the fact that the commanders tasked three policemen to guard the houses. Somebody did manage to set eight houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, your evidence was that the Croats, in some cases at any rate, protected the Muslims and Muslim houses; was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Three policemen from the civilian police force patrolled these houses non-stop to protect Muslim property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So the answer is "Yes." Your answer is "Yes," the Croats protected --

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We wanted to protect them, yes. We worked on it, to protect the houses, yes, yes, the Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Question interrupted by interpretation of previous Answer] ... questions by recalling your testimony.

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of any reverse instances in which Muslims protected Croats or Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: In Donja Veceriska, I don't know. When they left on the 18th of April, they started coming back, so in that month, I did not have occasion to contact any Muslims. Probably, probably there were individuals who did so in view of the fact that not all the houses belonging to the Miskovic family had been set on fire, which means that somebody had prevented them, somebody had prevented his fellow Muslim from setting fire to the houses. Somebody succeeded in protecting these houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that there were instances of mutual protection?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When asked to summarise your evidence, would you say that, so far as you knew, there were instances in which Croats protected Muslims and some reverse instances in which Muslims protected Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: We're speaking about houses in the testimony. Now, as regards the protection of Croats, that is, protection by the Croats, the nine Muslim civilians were protected to a maximum degree. Nobody in the combat activities had remained where the Muslims had control over Donja Veceriska in those two days, so that in actual fact, they did not have anybody to protect from the Croats. The houses were left empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you hear of any instances outside of your village in which Muslims protected Croats or Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What were relations like between the two communities before the conflict? Did they get on well?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, while there were joint patrols until the end of October 1992. That means we worked together. We would visit each other's houses. We would go visiting. We would socialise. For example, in my family, there are more mixed marriages than uni-ethnic marriages. My sister is married to a Serb, for example. My uncle's daughter is married to a Muslim. My uncle's son married a Serbian girl. My uncle's daughter is married to a Serb, once again. Two aunts have two children, and they married Serbs. So there are more mixed marriages than there are uni-nationality marriages. I don't know what the war brought with it. You are able to see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Indeed, we are, and you're helping us. Thank you very much. Let me ask you this last question: How do you judge as to the prospect of those relations returning between the three communities to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Relations can be resumed only if the extremists from amongst the Muslim people be held responsible here in The Hague and be brought to justice. If they are left to walk free, then we Croats will always fear them, and so only by taking the extremists into custody would we gradually be able to resume our relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You spoke of extremists amongst the Muslims. To your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- were there any extremists amongst the Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: Not a single Croat from Donja Veceriska was the perpetrator of any excessive behaviour, and if you don't do any excessive behaviour, I don't consider you to be extremist. But if you shoot and if you say to somebody's very eyes -- for example, the Muslim Suad Sesid and Ferid Kalca -- for example, two cases in point, and Ferid Kalca and Nahid Haskic said that Turkish times would be upon us and that they would sleep with our wives, then that is placing human dignity in jeopardy, because the Turkish times were a period when the Turks had the right on the first night of the marriage to sleep with our wives, and for me, that is extremist conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Should I sum up the last phase of your evidence this way, that your testimony to the Court is that there were extremists on the Muslim side, but there were no extremists on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: NIKICA LOVRIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side, not a single one. I said, when I testified a moment ago, that if you resist and say that the Turkish times will not come and that we're not going to wear fezzes and we're not going to use the Turkish terms "lahko," "mehko," they would say that you were an extremist, and it is not extremist if you defend your own human dignity. That's what I think at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Judge Rodrigues? I don't have any questions either. Once again, we would like to thank you. We'll ask you to remain seated for a moment. We're going to take a ten-minute break. Let me remind you that we have to finish at any cost this evening so that Mr. Plavcic can go home. Let me remind you that the examination-in-chief lasted for 26 minutes, and we will ask that you not go beyond 26 minutes, Mr. Cayley. We will resume at ten after six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Dubuisson. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Plavcic, thank you for coming back. I don't think it's going to take very long. Mr. Cayley, you've got 26 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good evening. Thank you very much for the Court's indulgence in giving me the additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Plavcic, good evening. My name is Cayley. I'm from the office of the Prosecutor. This is my colleague, Mr. Harmon. If I can just confirm a few biographical details to you. Prior to working at the Mediapan, did you work as a postman for the PTT?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a postman in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Subsequently, you worked as a doorman at Mediapan where your wife was a cook; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, prior to the break-up of the former --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes. My wife worked as a cook for a period of time, and I worked as a doorman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me in what year the HDZ party was formed in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope. Outside of the scope of direct. Let's at least stay within the scope if we're going to work at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's not waste any time. Mr. Cayley, just go ahead. The Judges will make their evaluation. Let's not waste any time today. I really want us to be finished this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Plavcic, when was the HDZ party formed in Busovaca; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I do not know exactly when it was formed, but it could have been in the '90s, maybe 1990. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you join the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not join the HDZ right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year did you join the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accords. I don't know exactly when. It could have been '94/'95.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your testimony is that you were never a member of the HVO political party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the HVO political party?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, what is that? Could we be specific? "HVO political party"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said earlier that he was never in the HVO military, and I believe I have a good-faith basis to ask the witness whether or not he was ever a member of the HVO political party, since my learned friend has often tried to distinguish, in some way, between the army and the political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no HVO party. Such a thing does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you can bring these questions up during the redirect. Continue, please. He's trying to find out what the witness did during the period that has to do with his testimony. All of you do that. You do that in the cross-examination and in the examination-in-chief. I'm beginning to understand the common law procedure now. Continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Plavcic, let me ask you a simple question: Were you ever a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I was never a member of the HVO because I'm completely unfit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Pero Susnjar?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Pero Susnjar, I know about this man. He's an elderly man. He's dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is he from your village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year did he die?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: He died before the war. I don't know exactly when but maybe even before 1990. I don't know exactly. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Ivica Andrijasevic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: He is the son of Stipo Andrijasevic. He's married. I don't know how many children he has, four or five now. He lives in Busovaca. I don't know exactly his address. He was in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1993, he was the commander of the HVO in Jelinak, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That is what I say. I don't know because I'm not a member of this HVO unit, but I know -- I heard from the others that Stipo Andrijasevic was the commander of the HVO in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, prior to living in Busovaca, you had lived in Jelinak for 39 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That is correct, from my birth until the conflict between the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the village of Jelinak consists of about 100 houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Approximately 100 houses. It could be a couple of houses -- a couple less, fewer than a hundred, and half of them were Croat and half of them Muslim. In the upper part of the village were the Muslims, and in the lower part of the village were the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think, having lived there for 39 years, you would have a good knowledge of all of the families who lived in the village. You would know both the Muslims and the Croats, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know Vinko Brnada?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Vinko Brnada, I know this man. He used to live awhile ago, how shall I put it, at the very top of the village of Jelinak, just under the Kuber, and then he moved to the village of Skradno at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1993, he was a member of the HVO, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Vinko Brnada, actually, there are two Vinko Brnadas. There's one whom I just mentioned, and there's another Vinko Brnada who is the son of Ilko whose full name is Ilija. He lived at Gavrine Kuce. At his age, he could have been a member of the HVO, and he was born there, so occasionally he would come to the village, but after -- so I saw him at that time, but after the conflict broke out, I don't know where he went and what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to cast your mind back to the end of January 1993. Now, this Court has heard testimony from two witnesses that an ultimatum was given to the Muslims to hand over their weapons to the HVO. What I would like to ask you is whether or not you are aware of a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the examination-in-chief was limited to only the 15th, 16th, 17th, and 18th of April, 1993 and no other period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I answered that objection, Mr. Nobilo. You are both right and wrong. You're right because the constituent texts says that the cross-examination must be matched with the direct examination, but you're also wrong because it would be an overly simple rule. It's nothing to bring in a witness and to ask only two questions, the questions which interest you, and for the other things that the Judges might be interested in to be hidden. So my job is to adopt the Rules to each specific case. I will remind Mr. Cayley if he is moving too far away from the direct examination, but for the Judges and for myself, there are certain things that we're interested in; otherwise, things would be too easy. You bring in a witness, you simply ask him about this glass of water, for example, and we never speak about the pitcher. That's not possible. All right. Mr. Cayley, I want to remind you about what you heard this morning. You have 26 minutes, and I want you to focus on the questions that were asked this morning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A meeting took place, did it not, at Pero Susnjar's house at the end of January where it was demanded that the Muslims hand over their weapons to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Since I was not part of the military structure, I did not have access to such information, and I don't know of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: No, I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hold any political advisory function within the HVO in Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to move forward in time to the 15th of April, and you stated that two HVO soldiers were evacuated through Jelinak to Kaonik, do you recall that in your examination-in-chief, on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: What I said about 15 April this morning was that when the shooting was heard in the area of Mount Kuber, this was early in the morning. At noon and in the afternoon, the population was being evacuated. As people who were not involved in combat operations, we did not know what was going on, and two HVO soldiers who were wounded at that time were brought through and on towards Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who did Slavko Garic tell that the Bosnian army had started the conflict on Kuber?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who asked him this question and what was going on, but there were several people there. They asked him, "What is going on? What is happening?" And he said, "We were attacked by the BH army." At that time, in fact, it was still called the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to him about this matter, about who started the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday in the Kupreskic case; do you recall you gave evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That I spoke to Gelic, no, I did not say that and I did not talk to him. I just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood me, Mr. Plavcic. Did you testify in another case in this Tribunal yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I testified because Madam Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac -- I don't know whose case I testified in. I just gave a statement what I did on the 15th, 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th, what I heard and what I saw on those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm just clarifying matters for the purposes of the Judges so that they understand that you've testified in another case. Let me ask you this question: Did you state yesterday the following: "On the 15th of April, I don't know who attacked whom because I wasn't there, I was in the village, and who was the one to carry out the attack, but when these people were evacuated, we heard the HVO was attacked by the army from the direction of Zenica." Did you say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that I heard fighting going on, this was in the early morning hours, at Mount Kuber, and over there, it was only possible for this to have been a conflict between the HVO and the BH army. I also said that those two wounded men were evacuated through Jelinak and that one of them said that they had been attacked by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What you're saying is that you did not say yesterday that you did not know who had attacked whom on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, before they arrived, I had not known who had attacked whom. When they arrived, I learned that the BH army had attacked the HVO, and I knew that there was shooting going on up there, and I assumed, I did not know this, but I assumed that the conflict was between these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that Muslim males were arrested in the village of Jelinak on the 16th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I am not aware of this. I don't know that they were arrested and anything in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Muslim males being taken from the village of Jelinak to the Kaonik prison in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: My apologies. Are you asking me whether I knew on those days -- do I know on the 15th? No. Do I know on the 16th? No. Later on, I heard that those Muslims, I don't know how many and who, had been transferred to the Kaonik prison. That could have been on the 18th, 19th, and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you heard that Muslim men had been taken from the village of Jelinak to the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, but I heard this on the 18th and 19th after I had fled. This is what I heard in Busovaca when I had moved far away from the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think on the 17th of April, early in the morning, 1993, 17th of April, 1993, you saw houses burning at the upper end of the village of Jelinak, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That is correct. In the early morning hours, that is, before the dawn, when we were being evacuated, that is, when we were fleeing the village, the Croatian civilians were fleeing, and I had not fled yet because it was easier to flee under the cover of dark, I saw the top portion of the village of Jelinak, that something was burning. I don't know whether these were houses or something else, but anyway, there was some light there because it was still dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the upper end of the village is the Muslim part of the village; is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, a witness has testified before these Judges that, on the 17th of April, the HVO were burning houses in Loncari; do you recall seeing that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not see this. Just as I said, I did not see it in the morning hours. When we fled, when we fled Jelinak village, Loncari was to the right of us at that time, and from there, we could see -- had anything been burning or had there been any military presence, we would have seen it, but we were just fleeing because we were shelled from mortars from Vran Stijene by the Muslims at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Mirko Jozic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Mirko?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Jozic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I don't know such a man. I've never even heard of such a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever take Muslim males from Jelinak to the village of Loncari and hand them over to Mr. Jozic to dig trenches in Loncari?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: No, I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 17th of April, 1993, I think you left the village of Jelinak at noon, at midday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: The 17th of April in the morning hours, that is when I fled Jelinak because of the shooting and all the explosions, and the war was raging. So after that, I did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At what time in the morning hours did you leave Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, in the morning hours, I don't know exactly the time, but it was not noon yet, so it was during the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you said in your examination-in-chief that, on the 18th of April, you learned that the HVO had lost control of the villages of Jelinak and Putis and that Croat houses were set fire to in Putis and Jelinak; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: It is correct that I said that on the 18th I learned -- I learned on the 18th that the Croats, that is, the HVO, had completely lost control of Jelinak, that the BH army had taken full control of the villages of Jelinak and Putis, and we also learned on that day that those two civilians were casualties, Anto Andrijasevic was wounded and another one was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see who set fire to these Croat houses in Putis and Jelinak? Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not see it because I could not see it. I left in the morning hours on the 17th, and at that time, except for what I have just said, that is, that in the uppermost part of the village of Jelinak, something was burning, but beyond that, I did not see anything. I also said on the evening of the 16th, I saw that in the village of Putis, in the upper portion of the village, something was burning also, and I could not see what it was because it was dark, and during the day, I did not look again. The village of Putis also has two parts, the upper and the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in your testimony, you were asked the following question by my colleague, Mr. Blaxill, and I'll read out the question: "In fact, would it -- to the best of your knowledge, Mr. Plavcic, wasn't there, in fact, just the area," and he's referring to Jelinak and Putis, "becoming a large battle zone with damage to both Croatian and Muslim properties?" Your response was, "That is correct, that on the 18th, all houses in the villages of Jelinak and Putis, in Putis, the Croatian houses, and in the village of Jelinak, all the houses were burning on the 18th. That's what I heard in Busovaca, that all the houses were on fire. Which were the ones to start burning first, I don't know. As far as I saw, it was the upper part of the village in the early morning hours that started burning first in the village of Jelinak." Do you recall saying that yesterday, Mr. Plavcic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: This is what I heard on the 18th. This is what I heard on the 18th, that all villages, that is, all Croatian villages, and Putis were set on fire, and what I saw, I saw in the early morning hours on the 17th, which is that something is burning, but I could not see what it was. It was still dark, and I couldn't see what it was. Also, on the 16th in the evening, in Dvor, which is the upper part of the village of Putis, I saw something burning, and the distance to there is about one kilometre, so it was a little bit above, and you could not see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Plavcic, a witness from the United Nations Protection Force has testified before these Judges that Muslim houses were plundered and looted and burned in Putis. Is that what you saw on the 16th of April, burning Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not see this. I did not see this on the 16th of April. That wasn't there, and I didn't see it. What I saw on the 16th of April, in the upper part of the village of Putis, which is called Dvor, something was burning, and in the early morning hours of the 17th, I also saw something similar, but whether there were houses that were burning, that, I did not know at the time. Eventually, I did learn that all houses in the village of Jelinak were burned down, both Muslim and Croat. After Dayton, when I went to the cemetery on the Day of the Dead, I went to light a candle on my parents' grave, I went to my house, and I saw that everything had been destroyed, except for two houses, Anto Gelic and Marko Vidovic's houses, which still had roofs and windows and doors, so they had not been burned down. They had not been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, another witness, another United Nations Protection Force officer, testified in this Court that on the 1st of May, 1993, he visited the village of Jelinak and was shown the site of a number of atrocities that were committed, allegedly, by the HVO against Muslim civilians in Jelinak. Did you ever hear about that in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I did not hear about that. I heard that there were dead on both sides because the fighting went on in the village itself, and they said that the fighting had been fierce. This is what I heard, but I did not hear specifically how many dead there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Mr. President. I think I'm dead on 26 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I admire your precision, and you have prevented me from being even more precise than you were, and I thank you for that. Mr. Nobilo, do you want to add a few things quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I shall also be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us return to the 15th of April, 1993 when you heard that fighting was going on at Kuber. Can you tell us, was this just shooting from artillery pieces or was there any strong detonation?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, that is to say, in the morning hours, there were no strong detonations. There was just fighting with artillery weapons -- all arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that before the 15th of April, that the HVO held positions on Mount Kuber?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard about this. They said that Kuber was under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Up until the 15th, the HVO had control of Kuber, and then you heard fighting on the 15th. What were you able to conclude from that fact? Who came and who attacked whom, before you received information from the wounded.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, I don't know how far I made myself understood, on the 15th up until noon, you could hear small arms fire. As the HVO was in control up there, then the other forces, the Serbian forces, for example, and the former Yugoslav army was not in existence there or in Zenica either, we were able to conclude that it was the BH army which had attacked the Croatian Defence Council on the 15th of April in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Judge Shahabuddeen? Judge Rodrigues? I have one question. Do you confirm that the upper part of the village was 80 per cent Muslim; is that correct? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. It's not very clear, but I can hear you. In the upper part of the Jelinak village, it was 100 per cent Muslim. There are two parts. The upper part, 100 per cent. It depends where you divide the village. But 100 per cent -- they are all Muslims up there and the lower part is only Croats. I just said, when asked about Vinko Brnada, that was a house that was far up, below Mount Kuber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: An UNPROFOR witness says that the houses that have been set on fire that were in the upper part, in principle then, that would be the Muslim part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Well, the possibility exists that that is so. I saw that something was burning. I didn't know whether they were actually houses. They could have been sheds, they could have been haystacks because it was night time. All you could see was that something was burning. But what exactly was burning, I couldn't see, because it was 300, 400, 500 metres away, and the terrain is not flat. So you couldn't really determine this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Whether they were fields or haystacks or sheds, that was in the Muslim part; you agree with me there, that's the upper part?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PLAVCIC (recalled)
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, yes. I agree absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We would like to thank you for having remained here all day long. This helped us to organise our work, and now you won't have to be here tomorrow. We have now concluded your testimony. The usher will escort you from the courtroom, but I would like to speak to the parties for a moment. So once again, thank you. We would like to express the Tribunal's gratitude to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will just keep you for another two or three minutes. Tomorrow we will begin -- Wednesday, we will be starting at 1.30 and not at 2.00. I would like to have things clearly confirmed by the Defence. After the testimony of the accused, there will only be two witnesses; is that correct? You asked for a video conference link testimony. This decision, has that been granted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the decision has been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So what witnesses will you have left, Mr. Hayman? Let us be very clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As to the video link witness, I believe the motion was denied. We need to make further inquiry. If the witness will not come to The Hague, as we suspect, then we will not be hearing from that witness, the Court will not be hearing from that witness. There is another witness. We are still trying to seek the ability to produce that witness. If we can get that ability, we intend to present that other witness. Those are the only two witnesses we are discussing, have any intention or hope at this time of calling in the trial. If we get a letter that informs us of something critical or important tomorrow, we will raise that with the Court, but we have no such information at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It would have to really be crucial, really crucial, and then the Judges would agree. All right. We now have a schedule that I will give you in closed session at another time because it still depends on a certain number of decisions that the Judges have to take. For the time being, we will say that there are only two Defence witnesses left plus the testimony of the accused. That testimony will begin at 1.30 tomorrow. Now here is my question, Mr. Hayman: Do you confirm that you need 35 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the direct testimony, Mr. President? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, for the direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not think we can complete the direct in 35 hours, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But that's what you said, Mr. Hayman. You've got to get into the habit of -- we have to get into the habit of carrying out what we say we're going to do; otherwise, we can't set up a schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: [Submission inaudible as previous comment was being interpreted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, there is a document that was provided in closed session which said that it would be 35 hours for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mean at the beginning of the Defence case, we estimated 35 hours for his testimony. That may well be true. That may well be true that in August, we estimated 35 hours for his direct examination, Mr. President. I can now say -- and Mr. Nobilo will be conducting the direct examination -- that I estimate the direct will be on the order of two weeks, and depending upon how many hours we get per day, it could be more or fewer calendar days. But, Your Honour, you may be well right that in August, we estimated 35 hours for the direct testimony which -- 35 hours at five hours a day is about seven calendar days. We think it's likely to be more like ten days, and I cannot give the Court a number of hours. It is too large a task for us to quantify specifically right now. We are going to try and go slowly so that the quality of the translation is at its absolute maximum, and it is going to take a couple of weeks, we think, for the accused to give his narrative of his experiences, his work during the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. I understand. I think I can speak for my colleagues, that is, as regards the rights of the accused, there is no question about limiting the testimony. I am asking the question solely so that we can set up a schedule that won't go drifting off, and all of us want to end this trial in an appropriate time period because everybody knows, you and the accused, it's been three years that he's been in detention. All right. We would agree then that we will specify the time as we go along, that is, after the first week. At that point, we will ask you to give a specific evaluation of how much time you're going to need for the accused. Would you agree with what I've just said? At the end of the first week of the accused's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will give the Court our best estimate at any time, Mr. President. If, at the end of five calendar days, we may well be able to give, by looking at Mr. Nobilo's notes, whether he's halfway through the volume of notes or one-third or two-thirds. That may be the most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- specific way to estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me now turn to the Prosecution. You, of course, will have the same amount of time for the cross-examination, that is, the same amount of time that was used for the examination-in-chief of the accused. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In principle, yes, Mr. President and Your Honours, but if we come across a situation like occurred with Brigadier Marin and we have a stack of documents this big (indicating) that we need time to review -- Mr. President, I think the cross-examination of the accused should be robust and it should be complete and it should not be constrained by any artificial time limits. In principle, Mr. President, we agree. We will try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I want to tell you in principle that there must be an exceptional decision on the part of the Judges, but in principle, you will have the same amount of time for the cross-examination. You have to choose your questions, as you did today. In principle, you have the same amount of time as was used for the examination-in-chief. We will not set the time today for the redirect. I think it would be superfluous and pointless to do it today. But we will do it depending upon the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, and then we can set the time for the rebuttal. During a closed Status Conference, that is, the Judges and Mr. Olivier Fourmy will give you an evaluation of the last phase of the trial because it should include the other sequences which include the rebuttal time and the rejoinder time, all of this based on certain criteria that we will inform you of. Let me turn to my colleagues. Unless they have any further comments to make -- Judge Shahabuddeen, Judge Rodrigues? All right. Having said this, we will see one other tomorrow at 1.30. Mr. Hayman, you have a question. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just to posit the issue, Mr. President. We certainly expect that General Blaskic will be able to testify from the witness box so that he can have access to the ELMO, and it is most appropriate, we think, that he be there and that he not have a security guard on each arm, that he have some reasonable space so that he can concentrate and feel the opportunity to communicate fully with Your Honours. I hope that's not a problem with the security department, but I raise it this evening so that the issue is out there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. We are totally confident in the accused. Up to this point, he has never demonstrated any desire to run away or to fight with his guards. We want him to be very comfortable so that he can express himself as well as he needs to express himself. You know, I don't come from a system that works with the accused in that way, that is, when the accused is a witness, but our rules do allow that, and once the accused is testifying as a witness, of course, his place would be there and he would not have guards. We will start tomorrow then at 1.30. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of February, 1999, at 1.30 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
